name: Luna 18 and Luna 23
short_status: Failure: two Soviet sample-return attempts that brought back nothing. Luna 18 crashed near Mare Fecunditatis on 11 Sep 1971; Luna 23 tipped onto its side landing in Mare Crisium on 6 Nov 1974 and wrecked its brand-new deep drill, though it kept transmitting for 3 days.
tagline: Soviet Union · Sample return · 1971 · The space race Failure
stats: of lunar soil returned by the two attempts combined
deep-drill reach Luna 23 was built for, and never used
Luna 23 touchdown speed, against a 5 m/s safe limit
lunar orbits Luna 18 flew before its fatal descent

facts.label: Luna 18 launch
facts.value: 2 September 1971, 13:40:40 UT, Proton booster and Blok D upper stage from Tyuratam (Baikonur Cosmodrome)

facts.label: Luna 18 orbit trouble
facts.value: Lunar orbit insertion on 7 September 1971 cut off 15 seconds early, leaving a wrong 100 km circular orbit; an attitude-control engine fault then blocked the nominal 16.9 x 123.9 km orbit, settling it into 93.4 x 180.3 km

facts.label: Luna 18 operations
facts.value: 85 communications sessions and 54 lunar orbits before it was commanded down toward the surface

facts.label: Luna 18 crash
facts.value: 11 September 1971: the attitude-control engine failed again during braking, the craft could not hold orientation, and signals ceased at 07:47:16.5 UT (impact, possibly ~100 m above the surface) in rugged mountainous terrain near the edge of Mare Fecunditatis

facts.label: Luna 18 impact site (estimated, unconfirmed)
facts.value: Tracked to roughly 3.57 N, 56.50 E; an LRO image shows a candidate crater at 3.76 N, 56.66 E, but the identification was still unconfirmed as of February 2020

facts.label: Shared design
facts.value: Both were Ye-8-5 family landers: 3.96 m tall, ~1,880 kg landed dry, 5,600 to 5,750 kg fueled at launch, with a 90 cm arm carrying a drill to core the regolith and a 39 kg return capsule

facts.label: Luna 23's new deep drill
facts.value: Luna 23 introduced the upgraded Ye-8-5M sampler designed to drill 2.5 m into the surface, far past the ~0.3 m reached by Luna 16 and Luna 20

facts.label: Luna 23 launch
facts.value: 28 October 1974, 14:30:32 UT, Proton from Tyuratam (Baikonur Cosmodrome)

facts.label: Luna 23 landing
facts.value: 6 November 1974, Mare Crisium, at 12.6667 N, 62.1511 E; came in with a vertical speed of 11 m/s against a 5 m/s limit and tilted 10 to 15 degrees, tipping onto its side and its sampling apparatus

facts.label: Luna 23 damage
facts.value: The hard landing depressurized the instrument compartment and knocked out the decimeter transmitter; the soil-collection device could not operate and no sample was taken

facts.label: Luna 23 survival
facts.value: The lander kept transmitting for 3 days; work with the station was ended on 9 November 1974

facts.label: Redemption 2.3 km away
facts.value: In August 1976 Luna 24 soft-landed about 2.3 km from Luna 23 (LROC-derived) and returned 170.1 g, finally proving the deep-drill design that Luna 23 was built to fly

timeline: Luna 18 launches on a Proton from Baikonur, a sample-return follow-up to Luna 16
Enters lunar orbit, but the insertion burn cuts off 15 seconds early and an engine fault leaves it in the wrong orbit
07:47:16 UT: attitude control fails during braking and Luna 18 crashes in rough terrain near Mare Fecunditatis
Luna 23, rebuilt around a 2.5 m deep drill (the Ye-8-5M), launches on a Proton from Baikonur
Comes down in Mare Crisium at 11 m/s, tilts 10 to 15 degrees and topples onto its sampler; the drill is wrecked, but the lander survives
After 3 days of transmissions from its side, work with Luna 23 is ended
Luna 24 soft-lands about 2.3 km from Luna 23 and returns 170.1 g, redeeming the deep-drill design
LROC images find Luna 23 lying on its side and fix the true 2.3 km gap between it and Luna 24
